Original synthetic data, not disguised observations.

The public edition uses new fictional case data generated solely for teaching. The generators stipulate distributions, coefficients, assignment rules and noise. They do not resample, fit to, or approximate the course’s earlier historical source records.

Names identify fictional scenarios, not actual people, companies, cities or markets. All displayed case estimates and chart values are calculated from the new generators. Pure mathematical examples and formulas are labeled by their role.

External data licensing is therefore not a prerequisite to running these public labs. Synthetic does not mean realistic, and a known simulation mechanism does not establish how any real system works.

Reproduce from a fresh environment.

Use Python 3.11 or later with NumPy, pandas, SciPy and scikit-learn. The repository records the tested dependency versions. No network is used by the labs after those standard packages are installed.

python -m venv .venv
# Activate the environment for your operating system.
python -m pip install -r requirements.txt
python scripts/build_all.py
python scripts/check_public_release.py

Run an individual downloaded script with Python, or open its notebook in a Jupyter-compatible environment. Run the code from a fresh kernel. Floating-point results may vary slightly across library versions, so compare to the precision shown rather than expecting identical last digits across every platform.

Use the examples for methods, not empirical claims.

Choose the real decision’s population, measurement process and assignment mechanism independently. A simulation can reveal an estimator’s behavior under its stated assumptions. It cannot prove those assumptions hold in a business, medical or policy setting.

The private historical course edition has not been overwritten. This public edition is a distinct teaching release with different data and recalculated results.

Further reading.

  • Békés and Kézdi: Data Analysis for Business, Economics, and Policy for applied analytical reasoning.
  • OpenIntro Statistics for statistical foundations.
  • scikit-learn: common pitfalls for validation and leakage.
  • Hernán and Robins: Causal Inference for causal identification.

These links are optional readings, not data sources for the generated cases. Their materials keep their own terms.

Learning access.

All text, answers, navigation, tables and downloadable files work without an account. Lessons are readable with JavaScript disabled. Charts have text descriptions and corresponding data tables. Roadmap links, answer disclosures and downloads are keyboard accessible. On small screens, open the lesson roadmap to choose a stop.

The website itself has no analytics, login, cookies, or answer-submission service. GitHub’s hosting infrastructure has its own privacy terms.
